speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is an issue in which I became involved very early in the debate, as early as November 8, 1984 when we first heard of the changes which the Government was making in the Unemployment Insurance Act and regulations. It was interesting to realize what tack the Government was taking in its approach. The Government obviously zeroed in on those on long term employment, such as people in the Canadian Armed Forces. Their benefits when coming out of the military into civilian life ended up meaning really nothing to them. They could not collect the full amount of unemployment insurance. I know of some of my constituents who got out of the Armed Forces and collected as little as $2 a week. Some of them got $16 a pay-cheque. The worst is that those changes were simply unfair.
Let us take a look at what went on in the longer process. The Globe and Mail zeroed in on these changes in December, 1984. It was an ongoing issue early in 1985. The first question I asked in the House was on March 26, 1985. I mentioned the loss of unemployment insurance benefits because of severance pay. That change was to become effective on January 1, 1985. Members of the Canadian Armed Forces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and others in positions where their type of occupation requires them to retire early get an annuity. You do not try at the time of retirement to describe the difference between an annuity and a pension because it is very difficult for anyone to understand. That issue also came up during the debate. Members of the Armed Forces or the RCMP who get out in their forties take a monthly pay with them.
The unfairness is not just the case that people did not qualify for full unemployment insurance once they got out of the service or whatever, but because they still paid premiums like everybody else. Their pension income or annuity, whatever you want to call it, was part of their pay package and agreement while working. But the Government is taking this away simply by changing regulations.
I remember many of us asking questions of the then Minister of Employment and Immigration, the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald). Time and time again she would repeat the dates on which various announcements were made. The announcements meant nothing. If she was going to change them, she said would announce them some time. It had nothing to do with the rationale for having done so. After she finished naming all the dates a number of times, she got around to saying that everything would be referred to the Forget Commission. I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) about it one day. He told me that it was a very complex problem and that it would be referred to the Forget Commission. That was his way out. But it was the Government that made the issue complex by changing the regulations in the first place.

June 9, 1987
Unemployment Insurance
Along the way we had a press report and comments emanating from the then Deputy Prime Minister, the then Member for Yukon and also from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) who disagreed with their colleague in Cabinet, the then Minister of Employment and Immigration. She still did not listen to them. Yet she would rise in the House and say that if the Hon. Member had representations to make or had any useful comments, she would be glad to receive them. I did not think there was much sense in me speaking my mind if she would not listen to her own cabinet colleagues who were speaking to her about it.
I appreciate the problem faced by the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie). He spoke very well on this matter this afternoon. For those of us who represent large military communities, it really created a great problem. Although members of the military community choose the ridings in which they vote, those of us who have large military bases in our ridings have many more such constituents than other Members of the House of Commons.
At that time, the Government's regulations denied unemployment insurance benefits to those military personnel who were paying premiums the same as anyone else. They were met with a double whammy. Members of the RCMP and the Canadian Forces, unless they get into serious difficulty, continue to be fully employed and, as a result, never make any demands on the Unemployment Insurance Fund. However, when they get out, they cannot collect the full amount of unemployment insurance benefits because the benefits they earned while serving those years were used against them. Actually, their own pay packages were being used against their ability to collect unemployment insurance benefits.
The Government attempted to hide its decision at that time by passing it into law through an Order in Council. It changed the regulations and effectively bypassed the House of Commons. These changes were brought in in such a way that opposition Members were prevented from debating them in the House of Commons. We woke up one morning to find that the Government had made all these changes in Cabinet and that we were suddenly faced with new rules for collecting unemployment insurance benefits.
We tried to tell the Government that if it could change the regulations to deny people benefits after they had paid for them, then it had equal authority to change those regulations back so that those people would be treated fairly and could collect unemployment insurance benefits when required between jobs. However, the Government never accepted that. It simply turned everything over to the Forget Commission.
The Government expected the Forget Commission to be the answer to all of its problems. We also know that when the Forget Commission dealt with these issues relating to unemployment insurance, it too disagreed on them. There was much dissension within the commission while the matter was being studied. In fact, two members of the Forget Commission
disagreed publicly with the changes the then Minister of Employment and Immigration had made. However, that did not faze her. She went on her merry way defending her defenceless position. Then the Government finally saw the light and decided to change those regulations much later on.
The regulation relating to members of the RCMP, the Armed Forces and others employed similarly has been changed but it is certainly not a very satisfactory solution. The Government has told those people that their pensions will continue to be used as income consideration when applying for unemployment insurance benefits. As a result, people coming out of the Armed Forces after January 5, 1986 will apply for unemployment insurance and will receive reduced rates because of the annuities for which they applied under their financial arrangements and pay packages throughout the years they worked. That is unjust.
Then there is a regulation that says that if those people get out of the Armed Forces, the RCMP or equivalent employment, and if they work the required number of weeks depending on in which region of Canada they live, they will be able to qualify without their pensions coming into play. The problem here is the fact that when many people get out of the Armed Forces, they have difficulties in civilian life. Many of them are trained soldiers. Some have held jobs that allow them to adjust easily into civilian life, but what happens to the people who are trained in fighting, warfare and handling equipment used in securing a country? These people may not have an expertise that would allow them to fit easily into civilian life. As a result, it takes them much longer to adjust from their old jobs to their new jobs. Surely during that period of time, that regulation should apply.
1 would like to see this regulation changed to allow for people who are in that position. Some of these people even have to take training after they leave their old jobs in order to get new jobs. Surely that should be taken into consideration as an added argument in favour of changing that regulation.
On Wednesday, May 14, 1986, an article appeared in The Globe and Mail bearing the headline "Ottawa determined to fight in growing battle over UI pay". It reads in part as follows:
The current 3,000 appeals will mushroom soon to about 30,000, said Ed
Halayko, spokesman for the Canadian Armed Forces Pensioners Association.
I would like to pay tribute to Ed Halayko today and to the Canadian Armed Forces Pensioners Association and other associations for the way they carried on this battle. They truly realized what this meant to people with whom they could relate very well and with whom they had associated every day of their lives.
Service personnel will continue to retire and to face this problem between retiring and acquiring their first jobs. I must ask the Minister a serious question, and it is one I have not heard him answer. Why should members of the Canadian Armed Forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police be required to pay unemployment insurance premiums if they
June 9, 1987

cannot make use of them in a better way than that which this legislation provides? That is the injustice of the whole thing.
I would like to put on record a letter from a member of the Canadian Armed Forces. It reads as follows:
I am presently a member of the Canadian Forces (CF) and have been for the past 26 years. My home town is Eston, Saskatchewan, and I am presently stationed at St. Louis, Missouri, U.S.A.
Here is a man who served for 26 years, who obviously never received a single UIC cheque during that period of time, yet paying premiums the same as any other Canadian, knowing full well when this came in that he could not collect the full amount at the end. I go on, Madam Speaker:
Approximately 20 years ago, it was legislated by our Government that CF personnel would contribute to the UI Commission with the understanding that CF members would benefit from the investment if required. As you are well aware, Mr. McKnight, CF personnel must retire early in life, (in my case 50 years of age) and seek continued employment because the CF pension benefits are not sufficient to survive in the Canadian economic system.
Being released from the CF at a relatively early age is a traumatic enough experience, however, to pay into an insurance system that will not benefit us while seeking new employment is ludicrous, not ethical, and against my human rights.
There is the precise message that the Government must get. There must be something done to make this system fair for members of the Canadian Armed Forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and others. We hear in this House of Commons about moral conduct. I say to the Government, Madam Speaker, that it is immoral conduct to charge people for something that they do not get. It is legal robbery in a real sense. Going on with this letter:
Generally, a member of the CF who retires with 20-25 years of service will not be eligible to draw any UIC benefits.
My second concern is that when I retire, and obtain employment, I will still be required to contribute to a system in which I will derive no benefits should I become unemployed.
At that time he was referring to his pension that would still apply. We have learned since that that has been adjusted somewhat, but it is still not fair, Madam Speaker. That person is still going to be affected during the most challenging part of his life. That is between his major occupational career and the next job, starting his second career.
We know simply that this Government got into a mess that it never thought it would get into. It is trying to crawl back out of it by leaving old inequities remain and creating new ones. As everybody in this House knows, this Government chopped $100 million out of the Atomic Energy of Canada Limited budget and wanted a cut-back in employees. It gave them the golden handshake, you know, "get out, we'll pay you to leave your job." About 550 employees have left as of this time or will leave very shortly. These people are being shoved out on retirement at an early age, again having paid unemployment insurance premiums all their working careers with that Crown corporation, and are not able to collect, Madam Speaker.
So what happens? I'll tell you. As the Member of Parliament for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke, which contains
Unemployment Insurance
Canadian Forces Base Petawawa and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited Chalk River where people are being pushed out to on retirement, I got a real education in the unemployment insurance regulations and a real education on how unsympathetic this Government is to long-term employees.
This legislation is far from perfect. If it is not fixed up by this Government, I hope it will be fixed up by a Liberal Government after the next election, putting some human feeling, common sense and honesty back into the system, saying to people "if you are going to pay for something, we are going to produce it for you." If that is not done, then no Government in Canada should be charging unemployment insurance premiums.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, the answers from the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands, the Finance Minister and the present Minister, those two in particular, were anything but satisfactory. The present Minister has done sort of a half job, a patch job of coming back and trying to save the face of the Government. But the face of the Government will not be saved until they put some integrity back into their own system.
Thank you, Madam Speaker.

speechtext:
Thank you for recognizing me, Madam Speaker. After two and a half months since Bill C-50 was tabled in the House for first reading, I am very pleased that we are on second reading, and possibly third reading today so that at long last the 1985 early retirees will be able to benefit and get their cheques at the earliest opportunity.
Madam Speaker, my colleagues in the House will remember that a few weeks ago the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) announced his intention to change the regulations on pension income so that all workers would be given fair and equitable treatment.
June 9, 1987

Under these regulations which came into force on January 5, 1986, any pension income derived from employment was considered to be earnings. In other words, the Government made it crystal clear that people who were going into retirement should not view unemployment insurance as an additional source of income.
The provisions of Bill C-50 with which I will deal today do not change anything to the Government position, and I want to make this clear from the outset.
The Government agrees that there is a basic difference between a person who retires for good and another who quit his job to begin a new career. Since people in the latter group, men and women seeking new challenges, continue to be part of the active population, we believe they should be entitled to full unemployment insurance benefits regardless of the pension income they might be drawing.
Just so there will be no misunderstanding, Madam Speaker,
I want to illustrate the consequences the new provisions of the Bill will have for certain retirees. In the case of a worker who retired in February last year and who applied for UI benefits pursuant to the January 5, 1986 regulations, his unemployment benefits would be reduced by an amount equal to his pension income. So far, no change.
But let us suppose this man found a new job in May, 1986, for example, and was laid off a few months later, under the previous regulations his UI benefits would have continued to be reduced to the extent of his pension income.
Madam Speaker, this is where we intervene through the provisions of Bill C-50 tabled on April 1. As a result, the worker whose unemployment insurance benefits would have been reduced because of his pension income will be entitled to a refund of the total amount withheld until then if his benefit period is based on ulterior employment.
The effect of this amendment is to make the changes in the regulations on pensions, which have been in effect since April 5, 1987, apply retroactively to January 5, 1986.
Madam Speaker, this legislation also affects those who applied for unemployment insurance benefits before January 5, 1986, and who were already receiving benefits by that date. When the regulations on pensions came into effect on January 5, 1986, retirees who were receiving pension income either lost their entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits or received reduced payments, so that the Government had to take action to ensure these people were treated fairly.
Madam Speaker, the Government acted as follows: The eligibility of these persons will from now on be determined according to the old rules. Let me explain. A retired worker whose unemployment insurance benefits were interrupted or reduced because of his pension income and who applied for benefits before January 5, 1986, will be reimbursed for the equivalent of the amounts previously withheld from his benefits. That is clear.
Unemployment Insurance
Furthermore, Bill C-50 contains another important change since March, 1985. A person who received severance payments upon termination of employment found that this delayed the beginning of his benefit period or reduced the number of weeks of insurable employment for his qualifying period.
Madam Speaker, according to the amendment proposed by the Government, separation payments will no longer reduce the number of weeks of insurable employment or the duration of the benefit period. We still abide by the principle that no one should be receiving severance payments and unemployment insurance benefits at the same time. I think that should be understood, Madam Speaker. However, in some cases such payments were spread over many weeks. In extreme cases, the simple fact of receiving separation payments spread over a long period could make a person ineligible for unemployment insurance benefits.
Under the new provisions, both the qualifying and the benefit periods of the claimants will be extended by the number of weeks corresponding to the moneys paid at the time of employment termination. Thus, most people in such a situation will not loose the protection of the Unemployment Insurance Plan at the time when they most need it. The new provisions will be deemed to have come into effect on April 5, 1987.
If I may, Madam Speaker, I would like to outline the three major changes proposed in Bill C-50 introduced in the House of Commons by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard).
Since April 5, 1987, workers who rejoined the labour market after retirement have the same rights to unemployment insurance as any other Canadian worker, whatever their pension income. I repeat that pension income will in no way reduce the amount of the benefits to which retirees who have rejoined the workforce would be entitled. The Government proposes to have this amendment come into effect retroactively. People in this situation can ask for reimbursement of the amounts kept back during an unemployment insurance benefit period which began after January 5, 1986.
The second change concerns retirees who receive a pension income and who had claimed unemployment insurance benefits before January 5, 1986.
When the amendments proposed by the Government have been approved, the former rules will retroactively apply to the entitlement of such claimants. The sums deducted from their unemployment insurance benefits because of their pension income will be reimbursed by the Commission.
Under the third amendment proposed in Bill C-50, workers whose benefit period would be reduced or eliminated because their severance pay is spread out over many weeks will maintain full entitlement. The qualifying and benefit periods will be extended by the aggregate of weeks represented by the severance pay.

June 9, 1987
Unemployment Insurance
Madam Speaker, by specifying the terms of payment and adjusting certain provisions of the Act to current economic conditions, the Conservative Government is showing flexibility, quickness of action and an open mind. Like my colleagues, I am firmly convinced that our unemployment insurance legislation now meets the expectations and needs of Canadians as well as it possibly can.
I was listening to the questions which my Liberal colleagues asked each other earlier. When someone is not satisfied with a decision of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, he can appeal to the Unemployment Insurance Arbitration Board. This is his right. If the decision of the Arbitration Board is not in his favour, he can also appeal to the Federal Court.
In the case of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, which comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Employment and Immigration, anyone who feels his rights have been infringed, whether by Bill C-50 or by anything else, is entitled to an appeal at these two levels.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in the debate today. We have been waiting a long time to carry out this debate. As Members of Parliament will be well aware, the legislation was first introduced on April 1, April Fool's Day. We all realize that the Minister is a jovial and funny fellow. He likes to tell stories and jokes. We thought he was pulling an April Fool's joke on the people of Canada. When he introduced Bill C-50, he said that some Canadians who had retired would receive the unemployment insurance benefits they had paid for. However, if one was going to apply after January 5, 1986, one would no longer be able to collect the unemployment insurance benefits for which they had paid for such a long time.
The people of Canada thought here is a funny Minister, this was a good April Fool's joke, only to find out it was not an April Fool's joke. The Minister was serious. The Government had decided that if an individual decided to retire earlier or was a member of the RCMP or the Canadian Armed Forces and, of course, was required to retire earlier than at age 60 or age 65, or if an individual was laid off because the plant or mine had closed and some severance pay was received, those individuals could not receive unemployment insurance benefits.
The people of Canada quite frankly could not believe the Government would do this. I remember delegation after delegation coming to my constituency office in Kamloops- Shuswap and delegations and rallies on Parliament Hill of people saying: "We cannot believe that the Government would introduce legislation that would be so unjust so as to treat some people one way and to treat other people in a totally different way". Some people who had paid into the unemployment insurance fund for their entire lives would not be able to collect unemployment insurance when they lost their jobs.
I think all of us can appreciate the frustration that these people must have experienced. It is as if we had paid car insurance amounting to hundreds of dollars every year in the event that when we are unfortunate enough to have an accident we make a claim and insurance will be paid to compensate for any loss. Similarly, in comparing the unemployment insurance situation to the car insurance situation, if one gets into a car accident then one goes to one's friendly insurance broker and says: "I am submitting my claim for this accident. I have been paying insurance to your company now many years". If the broker were to say: "We are no longer going to pay you. We have changed our policy, changed our mind. You seem to be someone who has an extra car, and you seem to have a good job. We won't pay you. Come back in a few months after you have exhausted all your funds trying to

June 9, 1987
Unemployment Insurance
pay for the damage to your car and we will see what we can do for you", we would laugh. We would simply throw our hands up in despair that the world had gone mad.
Such is the case with the Minister of Employment (Mr. Bouchard). He brings forward Bill C-50 which basically says that if one has retired from the Armed Forces, or from the RCMP, or if one has decided to retire early from one's firm to allow a younger employee an opportunity to come into one's line of work, then one would be penalized because one would not be able to collect unemployment insurance because one would be collecting a modest pension or severance pay. Until one has exhausted that amount of severance pay, or while one is collecting a modest military pension let us say, one's unemployment insurance would be deducted to reflect that. In other words, it would be considered as earned income.
I ask Hon. Members if they can imagine anything so peculiar. Here is an individual, let us say in the Armed Forces, who has been paying unemployment insurance for perhaps 20 years, paying unemployment insurance every week for 20 years. This person then retires, as people in our Armed Forces do after a certain length of time, with a modest pension. It is not enough money to live on.
Here are people from our Armed Forces who must go out to seek other employment, develop other careers, perhaps take advantage of some of the skills or expertise they have learned in the Armed Forces and then apply that to the civilian world. We all know how difficult that is, particularly if one lives in certain parts of Canada and finds oneself retired on a modest military pension and must go out to seek employment. That might take some time. In Kamloops we have just closed down a major military installation. It is very difficult for people in an area in which the unemployment rate is perhaps 15 per cent or 20 per cent to find a job right away. It might take a few months, if one is lucky. Well, in cases such as that, these people would not receive their full entitlement of unemployment insurance benefits because they would be receiving a modest pension. The Government has decided that if one is receiving a pension then one will have one's unemployment insurance deducted to reflect that amount of money since it is considered to be other earned income.
That is grossly unfair. People have been paying into this unemployment insurance for many, many years, with the assumption that when they did retire they would have an opportunity to have a few months, perhaps the better part of a year, to seek other employment. As I have said, in some parts of Canada that is a real challenge.
One must ask oneself: Why would the Government bring in such peculiar legislation? Why would the Government decide to penalize those people who are receiving alternative funds from pension funds, for example, or let us say from severance pay? Why would the Government do this? I suppose one could say the following. There must be a problem with the unemployment insurance fund. There must be a deficit situation.
Such is not the case. Certainly during the depths of the recession there were years when there was a deficit in the unemployment insurance fund. But I ask Hon. Members to consider these figures. In 1985-86 there was a surplus in the unemployment insurance fund of $174 million. In other words, of all the money taken in by UI, and in consideration of the money going out to help those who found themselves unemployed, there was a surplus of $174 million. That is a great deal of money.
In 1986-87 the figure increased to $720 million in surplus funds. For the present year, 1987-88, the projected figure is a surplus of $1.7 billion. That is an incredible amount of money. There is no need to become niggardly and to penalize tens of thousands of people who are already a part of a system today, let alone those who will be part of the system in the future, who have a modest income from a pension into which they paid for so many years and who now find themselves to be ineligible to collect unemployment insurance benefits.
I wish to make one thing clear at the outset. Bill C-50 will bring help to a number of people who were caught as a result of the Government changing the rules of the game half-way through it. About one-third of the 50,000 people affected will receive justice as a result of Bill C-50. But the question remains: What about all the others? What about the other two-thirds of the 50,000 people affected by this change of legislation, let alone all those from now on and into the future who will be affected by it?
As a Party we say that this is a very unjust Bill. It is unfair. It is discriminatory. It is undemocratic. We cannot support a Bill that can be described in those terms. We recognize that it will bring justice to a handful of people across the country, a few thousand people who were caught when the Government changed the rules half-way through the game.
The only thing we can ask is why on earth did the Government do this? Why on earth did the Government decide to discriminate so much against those in the Armed Forces, in particular, and those in the RCMP, and those on private or public pensions to which they have contributed for so many years?
Not everyone is caught in this situation, as we well know. For example, if an employee of a company or a professional decided to invest money, not in a company pension plan or a government pension plan but instead into stocks or bonds, or into property in Hawaii, Jamaica or wherever, and then collected revenues on that for retirement purposes, then one is not excluded. In others words, if that is how one obtains one's pension funds, then that is okay. One can collect that money and collect unemployment insurance as well. However, if a man or woman who served in the RCMP for so many years, served Canada in that respect, and contributed to the government pension plan, then that person cannot obtain full entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits once he or she retires and is seeking alternate forms of employment.
June 9, 1987

The whole thing is illogical. To me it reflects the reality of a Government that is in a state of total confusion. This is a Government that really has no idea what kind of a society it is attempting to support. This legislation supports those who obtained their retirement income from investment portfolios. It discriminates against those who contributed to company pension plans or government pension plans, as those people in the Armed Forces and the RCMP would obviously be doing.
In a sense this legislation places Canadians into two classes. There are those who contribute to their retirement years in one way versus those who provide for their retirement years in another way.
I wish to indicate another concern which I have. The Government received countless petitions with respect to this matter. I remember my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), who day after day with our colleagues in the New Democratic Party presented petitions to the House bearing thousands and thousands of names.
In fact, I remember a stack of petitions presented one day which included 19,000 names of Canadians who were registering opposition to this discriminatory, illogical initiative by the Government. Earlier I mentioned the large rallies on Parliament Hill of retirees who were opposing the imposition of this legislation. They felt that they had contributed to unemployment insurance and pensions all their lives, only to have the Government change the rules at the eleventh hour and keep from them what they believed to be rightfully theirs.
I should like to refer to the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council which tabled a report indicating the following recommendation:
That the Government not proceed with the announced changes in the unemployment insurance regulations scheduled to take place January 1, 1986 -
In other words, the actual advisory group to the Minister indicated that the Government should not proceed.
The House will recall the famous Forget Commission. A member of that commission, Mr. Roy Bennett, a former executive with Ford Motor Company, spoke out in February, 1986. He was reported in The Winnipeg Free Press as follows:
In hindsight, I think it would have been better had the Government not made those changes-
Those were the comments of a member of the Forget Commission. He indicated that the Government initiative in this case was not particularly good.
I should also like to refer to letters from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the then Minister of National Defence, the former Hon. Member for Yukon, Mr. Nielsen. In his letter, Mr. Nielsen said:
After considering the options available, I have now concluded that the only reasonable and fair approach is to seek an exemption for the Canadian Forces from those provisions beginning 1 January, 1986 that will require pension income to be treated as earnings for purposes of determining unemployment insurance benefits.

The Secretary of State for External Affairs went on to say in his letter:
As you are aware, because of the unique requirements of military service, members of the Canadian Forces are required to retire at a much earlier age than people in other walks of life.
He made the point that members of the Canadian Armed Forces ought to be excluded from this discriminatory, unjust, and illogical legislation.
The most interesting letter we received was from the Progressive Conservative Women's Association in Oromocto-Burton-Geary which passed a resolution calling upon the Minister of Employment and Immigration to withdraw the inequitable provision in the Unemployment Insurance Act. Even key players in the Progressive Conservative Party do not agree with this initiative of the Conservative Government.
One could identify individual Members of Parliament in all political Parties who have spoken against the legislation and have tried to point out to the Government that it was not an appropriate initiative.
As we all know now, it was an initiative announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on November 8, 1984 with no consultation whatsoever. We have been trying for nearly three years to determine from whom the Minister of Finance got the idea. To whom did he talk? Members of his own caucus, people in his own Party, people from all regions of Canada, and people from a variety of walks of life have unanimously opposed the legislation. One must ask with whom the Minister of Finance discussed the matter before he made the announcement on November 8, 1984 when he suggested that the Government should change the unemployment insurance program so that pensions and severance pay would be considered earned income.
I remind the Minister that for more than four decades the country has not considered pension and severance pay income as earned income, and the system has worked well. People have planned their lives with this in mind. People have planned for their retirement years with this in mind. For the Government to change the regulations-and I emphasize that point-is really a disservice to the people of Canada.
I must say that the Minister of Finance did not have the courage to introduce legislation to make these changes. He knew that if he were to introduce legislation at first reading, second reading, committee stage, report stage, and third reading, the people of Canada, through their elected representatives in the House of Commons, would have stopped that discriminatory, punitive legislation.
The Government chose the sneaky, underhanded, back-door, end run approach. It decided not to introduce legislation nor to propose statutory changes. It decided to simply rewrite the regulations in the Unemployment Insurance Act. This is backdoor legislation; this is under the table, back room, backhanded, sneaky legislation.
It indicates to me a Minister of Finance who does not have the courage of his convictions, or knows that his caucus would

June 9, 1987
Unemployment Insurance
not stand behind him, to introduce it as a Bill. Therefore, the regulations were changed behind closed doors. Unfortunately I suppose members of the Minister's Party now feel an obligation to find some way to support the legislation, as we have seen in today's debate. In a sense I feel sorry for a number of members of the government Party who must think of something positive to say about this initiative.
I want to say very clearly that as a caucus the New Democrats will not support the legislation today. We will oppose it on principle. We believe that we cannot support a Bill which treats people in an unfair and unjust way today and forever into the future.
We appreciate the Government's initiative will help a handful of people who were caught in the process prior to January 5, 1986. However, those who applied after that date are caught up in this very discriminatory Act.
I do not know how the Liberals will vote. I suppose, as some of their spokespersons have indicated, they will support the legislation. I do not understand why anyone would support it because of its very unjust nature.
I want to close by suggesting that another problem with the legislation is the fact that many people, who paid into the unemployment insurance fund and had their contributions matched by their employers, have waited for months and months for the Government to make up its mind, to make a decision on whether or not they would be eligible. As Bill C-50 indicates, a handful of Canadians will be eligible. What about the interest on that money? Tens of millions of dollars have been sitting in an account waiting for the Government's decision for months and months on end. However, there has been no commitment on the part of the Government to provide interest on those funds; these people have been unable to use that money. Again I remind the Minister of Finance particularly that when any Canadian owes the Government of Canada some money, interest payments are at the top of the list. The Government ought to do the same in terms of treating these people fairly.
In conclusion, I simply want to say that it is unfortunate legislation. Although we oppose it, we recognize that it will be helpful to a handful of Canadians.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today is a great day for our early retirees. After 17 months, their situation is about to be corrected at last. All who opted for early retirement before January 5, 1986, will finally be able to draw the unemployment insurance benefits to which they were entitled.
Madam Speaker, at this point, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Roberval and Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) for agreeing with the position taken by his Conservative colleagues who defended the cause of early retirees across Canada, and especially in Quebec, where there were quite a few in this group. The Hon. Member for Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup (Mr. Plourde), the Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne) and myself have, on several occasions, pointed out to the Minister the shortcomings of regulations that were adopted by this Government and which led unsuspecting people, to retire. They even received encouragement from their unions and some of our officials who said that if they took early retirement before January 5, 1986, they would be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits.
June 9, 1987

Madam Speaker, as a result, these people opted for early retirement, in the firm belief that if they did so before January 5, 1986, they would be entitled to full unemployment insurance benefits. In fact, what happened was that the pension income of these people was considered as earnings, and as of January 5, 1986, their benefits were reduced.
There had been some confusion in this respect, and at the time, these people were, I would say, unfairly penalized as a result of that confusion. And that is the position we took in explaining the matter to the Minister of Employment and Immigration and his predecessor, who had asked the Forget Commission to make recommendations in this respect.
Today, the provisions of Bill C-50 will correct this situation, and finally, early retirees who applied for unemployment insurance benefits before January 5, 1986, will have their entitlement fully recognized, and will be able to receive unemployment insurance benefits.
Madam Speaker, why did our Government have to consider pension income as income for the purposes of unemployment insurance? As you know, people used to retire at 65. So on that basis people were entitled to only three weeks of UI benefits. Gradually the mentality of Canadians has evolved and nowadays people retire much earlier. People began retiring at 64, then 63, and now we see some who retire at 60, 57, and so on. This is how Canadians came to believe they were entitled to one year's unemployment benefits on retirement. And of course we hear people say: I paid unemployment insurance premiums for 20, 25, 30, 35 years; it seems to me I should be eligible for UI benefits.
If we look at it this way, Madam Speaker, it does make sense that from a merit standpoint someone who has paid premiums should indeed be eligible.
But merit alone cannot be a consideration because the unemployment insurance principle is that people are entitled to benefits in cases of lost employment or if they are unfortunate enough to be unable to earn an income. This is where the Unemployment Insurance Act comes into operation so that people will have a source of income for a while, that is 60 per cent of their previous income over a certain number of weeks up to a maximum of 50.
The same principle prevails, Madam Speaker, except that the Government believes that unemployment insurance should not be considered to be a retirement income. So what we are doing is that in the case of someone who retires early, the unemployment benefits are reduced by an amount equal to what he gets at retirement, that is his pension income.
Madam Speaker, no one is being left out in the cold; no one is being left without a cent. Those who have no pension income and who are entitled to unemployment insurance benefits will still be able to claim unemployment insurance. However, those who have a pension income of more than $297 will have their unemployment insurance benefits reduced proportionately, which means that they might not receive any benefits. Once
Unemployment Insurance
more, our retirees are being protected as far as unemployment insurance is concerned.
Madam Speaker, the Forget Report recommended that the Government postpone this decision for two years.
I would like to remind my colleagues opposite that if our Government has done as recommended and simply postponed the debate for two years, some people would still have found themselves in the same situation when the legislation came into effect.
After the economic statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on November 8, 1984, everyone knew that the new regulations would come into force on January 5, 1986.
As I said at the very beginning of my speech, Madam Speaker, today is a great day for early retirees as those who retired before January 5, 1986, will receive the amounts to which they were entitled.
In addition, Bill C-50 now under consideration corrects another anomaly in the case of people who retire from our Armed Forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and later rejoin the labour market. Previously, their pension income had been considered as income when they claimed unemployment insurance. Bill C-50 now tells these people: If you rejoin the labour market and are eligible for unemployment insurance, your pension income will no longer be considered as income.
I believe that our Government is clarifying an important point which will solve the problems faced by these people who could not count on the protection of the Unemployment Insurance Plan after rejoining the labour force.
These are therefore the two major points of the Bill, and I would also like to remind opposition Members that in the case of people who may for instance have retired early before January 5, 1986, and may not have had the time to apply for unemployment insurance benefits, of course our Government has to draw the line somewhere. Whenever there is a legislation, the line has to be drawn somewhere. But those people are still free to present their cases to the unemployment insurance commissioners who will consider them on a case by case basis to determine whether those people are indeed eligible for unemployment insurance benefits.
Finally, Madam Speaker, I would also like to underscore the patience of our early retirees, for I have met with many of them in my region, in the Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean area, many ARSAC people and early retired pensioners, including someone from the Jonquiere constituency, Mr. Rosaire Bouchard who, on a number of occasions, contacted me to enquire as to when Bill C-50 would be introduced in the House. On each of those occasions, I insisted that we needed the co-operation of the Official Opposition to be able to introduce that legislation and make it possible for our early retirees, the 55,000 early retirees, to take advantage of the $295 million which will be made available to them.

June 9, 1987

I therefore want to acknowledge their patience and I regret that it took another two months before we could pass this legislation because of the unwillingness of the Opposition to co-operate.

Madam Speaker, if there is anyone in the House who has not been deafened within the last half hour, I would like to address a few remarks to them. The reason I rise is because I have an affinity for retired servicemen. As many Hon. Members will know, I served for 26 years in the Armed Forces and have some understanding of its pension system, more often referred to by servicemen as their superannuation.
When the new Minister was appointed a year and a half ago, I felt rather sorry for him. The Forget Commission had been formed and the only analogy I can think of for the job he had to do in trying to sort out the unemployment insurance system was rather similar to saying to him: "Go out to the kitchen. There is a stew boiling on the stove. Separate all the condiments in it without taking it off the stove". It was just an impossible task. The Minister understood that and is going about it one stage at a time.
I think 1 can speak for quite a few of the servicemen who say that this Bill is a considerable step forward to where they want to be. It will give them an opportunity which very few people have. After they qualify for unemployment insurance benefits, which is after 20 weeks, work at their second job, they can then get unemployment insurance at the full rate despite the fact their pension will be coming in at the same time.
Referring to pensions as earnings for unemployment insurance purposes is what this Bill is all about, whether or not we should consider pensions as earnings which, at present, we do. What has bothered me about this Bill is the anomaly in the logic which accepts that before the member retires, he must pay into unemployment insurance which is supposed to insure his employment. When he reaches retirement age, he must leave. He then retires and starts drawing his pension and suddenly he is not insured for unemployment insurance despite the fact he may spend the rest of his life unemployed and despite the fact, as I think everyone has pointed out, that during his entire service he would not have missed a single payment, or a single week's work, either. So it really is an exercise in futility. However, if an individual gets a job and holds it for 20 weeks, suddenly pension is no longer income. It seems to me that if it is logical to consider pension to be income in one period of one's life, then pension is income. Had the Government gone for that, I could understand the logic. Had the Government gone the other way and said it is not income at both times, I could understand that. However, to say it is income during the period that one is unemployed and as soon as one starts working again, it is not, is a bit hard for me to grasp.
I placed a question on the Order Paper in March. I do not know how many Members noticed. It was answered on May 4. My question was, and I quote:
In each of the years I9S5 and 1986, did Canadian Armed Forces personnel contribute to unemployment insurance and, if so,(a) what was the total
June 9, 1987

amount collected from them (b) did the Government match these contributions (c) what amount was paid out of the U.I.C. fund to unemployed exservice personnel?
The answer to the first question by the Minister for Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) was, yes, Canadian Armed Forces personnel did pay into UIC. He was a bit short of figures in 1986, having the "pay out" for 1986 but not the "pay in". In 1985 the servicemen themselves paid in $45,700,712. The Government contributed $56,988,788. I have never been able to understand in all the many years I have looked at these figures for civil servants, and this Bill applies to all civil servants, only to a slightly lesser degree because civil servants have an older retirement age than the Armed Forces.
I could never understand why the Government did not contribute exactly the same amount every year, but there is some technical reason. However, the fact is that the Government did not contribute anything in 1985. My question was: "What amount was paid out of the UIC fund to unemployed ex-service personnel?" The answer was $39,992,164 which is less than what the servicemen themselves put in. I think all of us in the House of Commons of Canada are smart enough about the way things are done to know that there is no fund sitting in a safety deposit box into which the Government put $56 million in 1985 because that would have matched the servicemen's input. There are careful records kept with respect to that fund, but it is not in existence. No bank holds it in bonds, nor is there anything that has been put aside to provide a fund which generates funds. Consequently, there are several theoretical billions of dollars in this theoretical fund.
The fact is that in 1985, in reality, the Government did not put anything into the fund. The serviceman and woman knows that he or she has put something into the fund because they can see it missing from their pay cheque every month. They put in $45.7 million.
If we look at 1986 we find out that this aberration, let us say, of the Order in Council, has been, to a large degree, fixed by this Bill. The payment out dropped from $39.9 million in 1985 to $28.1 million in 1986. The Government, instead of making only some $6 million from the servicemen themselves, made some $17 million. That is to what I object. I have asked the Minister to take that up and to reassess the entire unemployment situation. It badly needs it.
There are a great many people who are paying into the fund and a totally different set of people who are taking money out of it. It does not seem to me that that is the way that most insurance policies work. I think that the Minister has done the best that he could with this Bill. It meets the requirement that they be allowed to withdraw unemployment insurance if they are going into the civilian workforce. It will enable them to draw it at a better rate than other people who have similar incomes to what retired servicemen have.

Madam Speaker, I am glad to see representatives of our early retirees in our Gallery. They will be able to see for themselves the kind of procedural nit-picking opposition Members have been inflicting on us since last April, before we can finally make these payments.
The Government is hardly responsible for the fact that the debate and subsequent payments have not taken place sooner. We would love to adjourn this House immediately and order those cheques to be paid forthwith. However, for the sake of procedural arguments or because of a need to make a kind of circus out of the worthy cause of early retirees, the Opposition,
Unemployment Insurance
and 1 am referring to both parties, insisted on using all kinds of rules and regulations and procedural nit-picking to draw out the debate and try and enhance their political credibility.
Earlier, I met the leaders of the Association des preretraites in the lobby. They are starting to see the light and were wondering how useful what was being done today, and what has been done for a number of months by the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party, would be in getting payments to our early retirees who now will not be paid until next month, the eventual result of today's debate that was agreed to after endless pressure from Quebec Conservative Members.
I may remind the Hon. Member who moved an amendment just to draw out debate, an amendment by the New Democratic Party, that he doesn't seem to understand what the debate is all about or what the legislation is all about, and perhaps I could summarize the fundamentals so that he will have a better idea of what we are talking about.
The amendments to the provisions on pension income reflect this Government's conviction that retirees should not consider unemployment insurance as a supplementary source of income.
I think that is understood.
However, the Government recognizes the fact that a distinction must be made between those who retire permanently and those who retire in order to start a new career. I think that is also understood.
The changes announced by the Government make that distinction and ensure that people who retire and start a new career are treated justly and fairly, considering they continue to be part of the labour force.
When the Government learned on December 5, last year, that some people maintained they had not been thoroughly informed about the significance of the provisions on pension income which were to be implemented on January 5, 1986, we immediately proposed, at the request of the Conservative Members from Quebec, that the Government arrange to review the cases of those who stated that their decision to retire had been based on inaccurate information received from federal Government sources. A departmental investigation was carried out when we learned that some employees had misinformed the public. The Hon. Minister immediately asked for an investigation and set up administrative procedures. Because of the slowness of the administrative process, we found that application of these procedures could become very complex.
Once more, the Government took matters in hand to avoid complications, such as a possible difference in application of the rules from region to region, and made some changes to the regulations on pensions which had come into effect on January 5, 1986. Bill C-50 defines a simple rule, and 1 am surprised that the Hon. Members opposite cannot understand it. This simple and clear rule ensures fair treatment for all claimants during the transition period.

June 9, 1987
Unemployment Insurance
The rule is quite simple. All those who claimed unemployment insurance benefits before January 5, 1986, when the previous rules still applied, will have their elegibility determined according to the rules then in effect. In addition, all those who made their claim on or after January 5, 1986, will have their claims processed according to the new provisions. It seems to me quite clear that this meets exactly the expectations of the preretirees. This Bill was introduced in April, and if the Opposition had seized the opportunity to support the Government, these people would already have received their cheques. But no, they saw fit to play politics, play cat and mouse by resorting to procedural wranglings in committee, never failing to raise all kinds of objections or move amendments, so much so that after many months we are still fighting to get a green light to issue these cheques for which early retirees have been waiting for so long.
Hon. Members will recall that on December 5 our Government announced it was going to amend the legislation with respect to pension income. That was on December 5, 1986. While respecting the principle that retired people should not consider unemployment insurance as an additional source of income, the announcement made it clear that people who take another job after retiring and who stay on that job long enough to be entitled to UI benefits should not have such benefits reduced by an amount equal to their pension income. Again this was a request on the part of early retirees.
Through this legislation the Government will amend the pension income regulations as of April 5, 1987. In addition the Bill will make these regulations retroactive to January 5, 1986.
Again, that is exactly what our early retirees have been asking for and which they could get through some good will and gesture on the part of the Official Opposition.
These amendments will make it possible for workers, who have started a new career during which they have contributed to the unemployment insurance fund and who then find themselves without a job, to become fully entitled to unemployment insurance benefits calculated on their employment income following their retirement, whatever their previous pension income may have been. This is exactly one of the claims which is now being met by the Government.
This legislation deals also with a matter of equity, which has to do with the treatment of the amounts paid upon separation. Hon. Members will remember that on March 31, 1985, amendments were made to the treatment of amounts paid upon separation for unemployment insurance purposes.

Madam Speaker,
I appreciate the opportunity to join in the debate on this April Fool's Day joke which the Government has played on the workers of Canada who are anticipating retirement and wondering how they are going to handle their affairs. I appreciate the opportunity to say something immediately after the unseemly display which has occurred in the House, precipitated by an Hon. Member suggesting that the Opposition was holding up action on this Bill. Here we have a mess created by the Government in the fall of 1984. It has taken the Government months, years, one could say to recognize it as the mess it is even when the Ministers of the Cabinet pointed out the mistake which had been made.
Members on the front bench of the Government caucus are prepared today to indicate how unsatisfactory this Bill is even now. We then have a Member of the Government, a new member admittedly, since the 1984 Parliament, suggesting that somehow or other the Opposition has been holding this up. I can appreciate why a Member would be tempted to say that is a lie because it is not true. What we have to recognize here is a mess that the Government created and which it is refusing even now, belatedly in this April Fool's Day joke Bill that it served up, to do justice to Canadian workers.
What did we have? We had a new Government, swollen with numbers, arrogant in office, convinced it could do anything, dedicated to one end alone, convinced that only by means of reducing government expenditures could it return the country to prosperity and, regardless of any sense of honour, any kind of promises given in the election campaign, determined to do anything to reduce the outflow of government expenditures in various areas.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in preparation of his statement for presentation within days after the House convened in November of 1984, came up with a bright idea to change fundamental rules in the unemployment insurance system. It is a system which, at that point, was almost half a century old. It had been won by years and years of labour in the 1930s, in years of depression, by workers who were out of work and who wanted it, insisting that unemployment was not their fault, that governments had to recognize some responsibility. There were people in province after province who insisted that an unemployment insurance system was necessary on a national basis in order to provide for the unemployed. Finally, by constitutional amendment no less, the Canadian people resolved to do just that.
In 1940 unemployment insurance was added to the list of federal responsibilities. Fundamental rules were established for it. It was a system of insurance which was maintained by employees and employers. Government came into it when necessary to keep up the amount of funds needed to maintain the scheme. But it was a system of insurance.
In recognition of the plight that workers faced when they retired, there was a system of benefits laid out. In the 1970s that system of benefits was improved and enhanced at a time when unemployment rates ran very high and such a scheme was necessary.
What did the Minister of Finance decide to do in November of 1984 but to change the fundamental rules, to say that there are some lucky people out there who, when they cease to be employed, have money. In some cases they may become eligible for benefits. They may be eligible for severance payments. They may even have holiday pay. The Minister said: "Let us count all of that as income. It is marvellous. We can postpone the day when the unemployment insurance fund will need to advance anything toward them, when they will have any kind of eligibility for benefits. In the process we are going to reduce the outflow from the unemployment insurance fund and the deficit will be reduced somewhat".
No regard was given to good faith. No regard was given to the situation of workers who had earned these benefits over months and years of service. They were simply struck away. The philosophy of the Government was to break faith and save money.
What we have had is a system in which as many as 55,000 Canadians have been retiring just on that one aspect alone. Thanks to these changes the Government has been able to save
June 9, 1987

$250 million on an annual basis. Sure, it has been a nice saving. Yet no regard was given to the fact that the Government has resources that people put out of work do not have.
No regard was given to the fact that persons who had planned for years found themselves faced with retirement, involuntarily in many cases. After all, it was the military personnel in the Canadian Armed Forces, and others in the RCMP, particularly in the lower ranks, who were forced into retirement. This was not a voluntary decision they made. They were forced into retirement.
The Minister of Finance, having regard and responsibility for the finances of the country, and having the resources of his Department and of the Bank of Canada, as well as the Canadian people behind him, turned to these people who were forced by the regulations of the Armed Forces and RCMP into retirement and said: "You are not going to have any entitlement for unemployment insurance because your pension is too high". Or he said: "You may have a little bit of entitlement. We are going to take your pension benefits first and calculate them. If that is less than you are entitled to under the new regulations, we will top it up a little bit".
To say that to people who still might be in their forties or early fifties, people with responsibility for families, with children in college and university making large demands on their families, people who served the country well for decades was one of those fundamental acts of bad faith that has been characterized by Government time after time. It went on to characterize it over the next months. It aroused the anger of the Canadian people. It has provided the basic reason that has driven this Government down toward 25 per cent and less in the public opinion polls. That kind of lack of faith was not to be tolerated by the Canadian people.
What do the Canadian people do now but wait quietly for the day when they will have the chance to turf this Government out and throw it as far as they possibly can. That was the situation created by the Minister of Finance in the fall of 1984. It was obvious that it was a bad piece of work. It became obvious very quickly as the Minister of Employment attempted to work with the regulations and had to change deadlines. These were deadlines that were in effect for the end of the year, and then pushed back for later in 1985. Then further changes pushed them back until 1986. It was obvious that a fundamental mistake had been made.
In fact, ultimately, when the royal commission which was looking at the entire unemployment system declared in its report that a mistake had been made, there could be no doubt that the Government had taken the wrong course of action in the fall of 1984 in terms of this particular action for retirees. It was the minority report on unemployment insurance written by Frances Soboda and Jack Munro which drove the point home in paragraphs that considered not just retirement but severance payments and vacation benefits as well.
I wish to read some of this into the record since it makes the point so well.
Unemployment Insurance
Pensions, severance pay and vacation pay have one thing in common. They were all earned prior to separation from employment.
Pension income is a payment from a fund that was generated for an employee while he or she was employed. Vacation pay is an entitlement that is earned while employed and banked either in a "time off with pay ' bank or in some cases in a vacation pay trust fund. Severance is a compensation to long-service employees for their lost employment rights. It is earned while employed and paid out on termination to finance the special adjustment problems that older workers face. It is an asset, not income. These earned benefits are caught in the regulation's net because they happen to be paid out on termination of employment... It is illogical to treat them as if they were.
It is also extremely unfair. Many working people have taken early retirement from jobs in heavy industry, in particular, on the assumption that they could be able to supplement their pension income with lower-paying jobs after retirement, and that they would be eligible for UI when they were unemployed.
Thousands of others in the armed forces and police are required to retire many years before normal retirement dates. These "retirees" are expected to find other employment after "retirement." Counting their pensions as income makes them effectively ineligible for UI.
It is the only form of income not related to current earnings which is allocated against UI benefits. Investment income or income from RRSP's which is indirectly related to employment, prior to termination, is not allocated against UI benefits.
It is inequitable to count pension income against benefits, for example, but not RRSP income. It is inequitable to count severance benefits against UI benefits but not the proceeds of RRSP withdrawals or other forms of pre-termination savings.
There, in one of the distinctions which the regulations drew, we see the kind of unfairness that the Government was prepared to create. Those who were not able to deposit to a regular pension fund, those who had to use RRSPs, or those who built up investments through other means and who might well not be compelled into retirement, those people would have escaped the net anyway. Others, those thousands of Canadians who were grateful for pension plans, worked through their unions and by other means to build them up, built up a benefit, built up an entitlement for their retirement.
In cases where they were in the forces or with the police, very careful planning was required. I know about some of this from members of my own family. They made calculations on how they might use pension benefits, together with other sources of income, to find work and to continue in a productive role in society after they had retired from the forces.
All this was done away with by a sentence or two in the statement of the Minister of Finance in November, 1984. For years the Government has allowed the situation to prevail. It has allowed this abomination on Canadian workers to continue. Finally, we had the Bill on April 1, and the Government waited through April, through May, and more than a week into June to bring it forward for second reading.
We have an understanding that it will be debated at second reading and considered in Committee of the Whole, that we will have an opportunity to put forward amendments in an attempt to improve it. God knows that the Bill needs improvement. It should not be passed in its present form. I am sure the critics in our caucus and those in the Official Opposition want

What are we faced with? We are faced with Conservative Members who have something half good enough for them to want to make speeches about it. They want to spend all evening talking about it instead of giving us an opportunity to try to improve it in Committee of the Whole.
They are prepared to accept something which will save
22.000	workers on an annual basis but will leave another
33.000	workers unprotected. If they are prepared to make big speeches about it and fill the evening praising the Government for half-hearted measures a third of the way along the road, I suppose that is the situation in which they find themselves in government these days.
We all know that organizations of retirees across the country are not content with this Bill. As soon as the Bill was tabled they made clear that it was inadequate and insufficient to allow persons who were fortunate enough to find a second job to establish unemployment insurance eligibility by those means.
It is a classic piece of unfairness. Those who have connections, those with skills, and those who live in parts of the country where jobs can be more readily found are the people who are favoured. They might conceivably be able to obtain a contract for enough months to establish eligibility. However, those who live in Atlantic Canada, those at lower ranks in the forces who are unable to obtain contracts, and those without jobs wherever they are, remain out of luck. This is from a Government which claims to have the most needy always in mind when dealing with social policy.
It is an instance of Conservative unfairness and readiness to stick it to the unfortunate while pretending that the Bill which has been put forward is some great improvement to the unemployment insurance system. They have hardly begun to walk the road back to justice for the workers of Canada, for those who are forced into early retirement.
I see no reason for us not to get into Committee of the Whole as quickly as we can to put before the Minister amendments which would make the Bill what it should be, if we are to have a genuine return to the regulations that prevailed on November 7, 1984 and a return to the kind of justice the people of Canada want. Let us get to that point this evening and forget about speeches in support of something that does not deserve praise.

Madam Speaker, what would the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) have had us do in the fall of 1984 when we faced a very serious crisis? We had 1.5 million people unemployed and an unemployment fund which was empty. It was in deficit by at least $1 billion. This is what triggered the effort to try to resolve the problem.
The Hon. Member has seen what the Forget Commission recommended as a way of dealing with the problem. They were Draconian measures which would have either delayed the
payment of unemployment insurance or would have narrowed the number of weeks when people could have drawn unemployment insurance. They were unacceptable alternatives.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) looked at how we could put the unemployment fund on a basis where it could meet the needs of the unemployed and how we could create jobs to reduce the unemployment figures.
That is exactly what we have done. Granted, the unemployment fund can no longer be used as a retirement plan, but it was never meant to be a retirement plan. We did the best we could with a very unfortunate situation. The previous administration knew about the problem in 1982-83 and did absolutely nothing. We came along and had to do something about it. We felt that the most just thing to do was not to take away unemployment from people who were truly unemployed, not to make them wait longer, not to give them less money, and not to give them benefits for a shorter period of time. We looked at how the plan was being used in ways for which it was not meant when it was instituted.
The Hon. Member gave an historical rendition of what the plan meant, but he omitted a very recent piece of history. The fund was empty. What would the Hon. Member have us do? Would he have us shorten the period, give less money, or ask for more money from workers to put into the fund?
Now that we have this situation, would he have us not give a chance to members of the Armed Forces who usually take an early retirement, not because they have to but because they have decided that they can retire at 45 years of age? Would he have us not give them a chance to reapply for unemployment insurance? Would he not give a chance to public servants who want a second job after they have retired? Would he not give them a chance to have unemployment insurance? What is it that he would like us to do?
