speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to add my comments to those of previous speakers and give you my impressions of this Bill.
However, I must say, first of all, that after listening very carefully to what was said by the Hon. Members for Jonquiere (Mr. Blackburn) and Richelieu (Mr. Plamondon), that I have seldom heard so much political rhetoric in just two speeches.
Madam Speaker, since the Hon. Member for Richelieu finished his speech saying that he had met a philosopher who said that if you didn't understand the situation . .. I'm afraid I don't have the exact words, but perhaps the following saying will do. Speech is silver and silence is golden, if you don't want to make a fool of yourself. I think that what was said by the Hon. Members for Richelieu and Jonquiere was a clear indication that they don't know what they're talking about, and that the whole point of their speeches was basically to use an issue that is of fundamental importance to so many thousands of people as an excuse for political rhetoric. To consider the facts in chronological order, we have to go back to

June 9, 1987
Unemployment Insurance
November 1984, when the Government published a policy document under the title: A New Direction for Canada. This document was supposed to provide a plan and a timeframe for what was supposed to happen when, and to whom. So we get to the magic date and this particular group of Canadians is told that from now on they are no longer entitled to full unemployment insurance benefits, since any benefits they receive from their employer will be deducted.
This was in 1985, Madam Speaker. Today, in 1987, we are finally going to be given a chance to deal with a situation that has been dragging on for too long, and which in many cases has become a very serious problem.
Madam Speaker, as a result of endless protests, hundreds of petitions and numerous visits to Ottawa where people tried to get something done about this disgraceful case of discrimination, the Government finally showed its true colours last April. In April, it announced what it intended to do about the situation, after giving us all kinds of tentative solutions, none of which made much sense. In April the Government made its intentions clear when it tabled this Bill.
Quite recently, hardly 10-odd days ago, we were told: Listen, you in the Opposition, here is what we intend to do. So what is the reaction? We responded: In the interest of all these tens of thousands of people, as far as we are concerned we would have liked to have several days to debate this important question and the many injustices it raises; but in the interest of the tens of thousands of Canadian men and women who are frustrated and are waiting for fabulous amounts, we are prepared to co-operate to dispose of this matter in one single day. This was about ten days ago, Madam Speaker.
On the other hand, keeping in mind what I have just said, the first Government proposition to the Opposition on such a major issue was to hold the debate on this Bill on a Wednesday. And, as it happens, Wednesday is the shortest day of the week. And then they will claim, as did the Hon. Member for Jonquiere, that this is a great day for retired people.
It is a great day for retired people. First retired people can rejoice, second Government Members take credit for this decision which is woefully incomplete in many respects. They take credit for being responsible for this great day. However, if we had to define demagogy, I suggest this would be a good example.
The Hon. Member for Richelieu said that if the Government has been unable to deliver the goods until today the blame rests squarely on the Opposition. We were quite ready and we reacted immediately, as he said himself; we reacted immediately. This is June 1987, yet the problem dates all the way back to January 1985. So I would suggest that in either case Canadian men and women can see through such puffery, they will decide for themselves who is really guilty, who is really responsible for what, in my judgment, is indeed a black mark against this Government.
Madam Speaker, in my constituency and my own region, there are certainly about 400 or 450 Canadians who are directly affected by this Bill. These people have been waiting for months, more than a year, for the Government to give them what they were fully entitled to receive. These 400 people, at an important time of their life, made a decision based on what they were expecting to get, after examining the situation objectively and taking into account a very important factor for the economic well-being of their communities, as they saw that they could leave the labour market so that more young people could keep their jobs and support their families. For these 400 people, full unemployment insurance benefits were essential and even vital.
Suddently, they found that they had to make due with benefits which had been reduced, in many cases, to nil. Most of these people had contributed to the unemployment insurance plan for 20, 25 or 30 years and they were suddenly being told: You are no longer entitled to these benefits, or if so, only marginally.
It is only after being subjected to petitions, pressures and aggressive demands that the Government reversed its stand two, three or even four times, to give us finally what we now have before the House, namely Bill C-50.
Madam Speaker, I believe that all those who have been waiting for redress since their benefits were cut off are in the best position to understand who is responsible for this completely unacceptable situation.
We in the Opposition were and still are willing to co-operate. We shall co-operate as concerns the Bill which was called earlier today, and when the House adjourns this evening, the matter will be definitely settled and the people involved will be able to receive their cheques within a few weeks, at least 1 hope so. Among other things, this will be an opportunity for the Government to show it was serious when it spoke today about understanding and about generosity for these people who have been waiting for over a year because of these reductions.
In many respects, Madam Speaker, it would have been interesting to devote more than one day to this issue. We understand the extreme urgency of disposing of this Bill, so that the cheques can start going out as soon as possible. But having said that, I would be remiss if I did not indicate to you and to those concerned with this issue that it would have been important and even most relevant to keep on discussing this important and a number of its ramifications. I am referring here to the issue which I would described as discriminatory, most unfair and outright unreasonable. I had an opportunity before to demonstrate this point.
Let us imagine two Canadians, one working in the footwear industry, and the other in the manufacturing sector. Most everybody will recognize that in the footwear industry, salaries are somewhat average, not to say small in most cases. Clearly, Madam Speaker, an individual earning a modest salary does not have $1,000, $1,500 or $2,000 at the end of the year to
June 9, 1987

invest in an RRSP. He is at the mercy, in a slavish sort of way, of the pension fund which his employer has established for his employees. Contributions are always based on the salary earned, the generosity of the company's financial statements, so that pension funds which are made available to employees are generally quite modest. I am referring to the first individual to which my example applies.
The other one, who worked in a factory and had been fortunate enough to contribute to a pension plan, seeing what is happening here tonight, will not try to negociate his participation in a private pension plan but will prefer and rightly so, to take the money he was prepared to invest in that plan and put it in what is called a RRSP. When they reach 55 years of age, both men will retire and to ensure their subsist-ance, they will depend exclusively on the pension paid by from their employers, which consist of contributions taken from their pay cheques during 25 years.
No need to say that that pension doesn't represent much and is hardly enough to live decently. After a whole life spent on a low paying job, all the worker can count on for his retirement is a limited income. In a context of social justice, he could also reasonably expect one year of unemployment insurance benefits. But it will not be the case under this Bill because this man will be told: "That's it, you earn $300 a month, we deduct it from your benefits and we give you the difference." In his case he will live way under the poverty threshold while the other man could earn a more reasonable income and invest $1,000, $1,500 or $2,000 in a RRSP every year for about 30 years. That same worker who from the start, could look to a rosy future, will go to the unemployment insurance office to withdraw the full amount of his contributions; as I said, these will be higher than the contributions of his fellow worker who working in the footwear industry was paid smaller wages and we know that UI contributions are based on the salary earned. We have here a perfectly clear example, Madam Speaker, of totally unjustified and injustifiable situation, an absolutely discriminatory situation which would have warranted explanations and answers.
There is another situation which seems to be unbelievably unfair, and which is documented in dozens of files in my riding office. When plans were made by asbestos mines to lay-off workers, and hundreds of people were concerned, they had obviously been scheduled over six to 10 months. Those in managing positions with the company knew very well that they would be laid-off as of a certain date, while their colleagues were laid-off at a much faster rate and more expeditiously. From this group of employees who knew officially that they would be laid-off on a permanent and definite basis, a few left before the week of january the 1st; they had known for one to three months beforehand that they would be permanently and definitely laid-off. But in fact they were laid off in the first week of January. Everybody knows there is a two-week waiting period. Everybody knows that these about to be laid off, do not exhaust their holidays but keep them in order that immediately after being laid off they can count on a full salary which is
Unemployment Insurance
equivalent to paid holidays. Consequently, logically and mathematically, these people could not go to the UI office and file their claim for benefit. What happened? The legislation says, and very clearly contrary to many speeches we heard so far, at Section 4, paragraph (a): The Commission shall consider the entitlement to benefit of any claimant who made an initial claim for benefit before January 5, 1986.
For many, this legislation and its consequences represent a considerable improvement because it means several month qualifying periods, but for many whose situation I just described, there is no remedy to their problem, yet they are affected by the same situation of economic disaster in some area. Since they could not, because of a combination of circumstances, file their claim before January 5, the Government says: No, a line must be drawn, and they use as an example the fact that at age 65 one is entitled to old age security pension, but not at age 64, 11 months and 20 days. I accept that first example but I sincerely submit that in such a specific case, the individual who knew before January 5, 1985 that he or she would be laid off on a given date should be considered as all others who had the privilege, because it becomes a privilege, of filing an application before January 5. There is also the great injustice toward those who will be contributing thousands of dollars in unemployment insurance and who at the proper time will apply to obtain benefits but will be told: "Well, listen, you belong to a special group. You are not entitled to benefits unless you do this or that." Once again, Madam Speaker, it is an injustice, a discrimination and we would have liked to redress those grievances under a reasonable legislation which would have been fair and equal for all. We are told, and it was mentioned in a question, that for financial reasons, choices and restrictions had to be made as a result of the debt. On the other hand, billions are going to be spent to modernize defence while those individuals are entitled to expect minimum living wages. Such minimum living wages could be granted to them under a legislation which could be more reasonable and fairer.

pension income. This is to point out that unemployment insurance income is unemployment insurance and not pension insurance, as 1 said.

As you know, Madam Speaker, my colleague from Richmond-Wolfe started earlier by quoting a famous author whose name he did not mention, but who said more or less: Better shut up and look dumb than speak and prove that you are. And that is what the Liberals have done over the years.

I therefore fail to understand, Madam Speaker, why some Members, at least Members of the Official Opposition, said earlier today in this House: "Madam Speaker, it is a shame to see an irresponsible Government cause such irretrievable harm to the community of early retirement pensioners of Canada".
That shows one thing, it shows that opposition Members have short memories. Very very short memories. I want to remind them, Madam Speaker, that salaries and pensions were frozen at 5 per cent and 6 per cent while we had an inflation rate of 11 per cent, 12 per cent, 15 per cent. Madam Speaker, when the Liberals at the time took that action, when they did that to the Canadian people, I never saw, and I have read the proceedings, 1 took the trouble to read the proceedings of the House at the time, I have never seen any Liberal Member or Minister stand up and tell the former Primer Minister, Mr. Trudeau: "Look, what you are doing is not fair. You are hurting Canadian people. You are doing away with the basic rights of early retirees. You are removing fundamental rights from workers, mothers, and the economy".
June 9, 1987

No, Madam Speaker, all the Liberal Members, the 74 blockheads, as they would often be called by Mr. Parizeau, the former Pequiste Minister from Quebec, sat quietly in their chairs and said: "Our Prime Minister is right. I listened this morning as my colleague from Montreal- Sainte-Marie made this outrageous statement to the House: "Madam Speaker, the Gulf refinery in Montreal was closed by the Conservatives. No Liberal Member, no Minister, Madam Speaker, rose to tell his or her Prime Minister, Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources or Minister of Employment and Immigration: "What are you doing for our workers?" None, Madam Speaker!
Today, in this House, in the country, some are talking about social justice and equity ... We realize, Madam Speaker, how gifted the Liberals are in the art of deceit, how inconsistent they are in their actions to defend the interests of the Canadian people.
We must accept one thing. When we assumed power in 1984, we had some constraints, administrative constraints, a huge deficit due to a large degree to a careless administration, a deficit, Madam Speaker, which will mortgage for years to come future generations, my children, your children and their children.
Their mind was set on the short term, and on their own reelection instead of, the middle and the long term and the better interests of the Canadian people.
We will probably not have to remind them that they were the ones who allowed those at the top of the salary scale not to pay any tax. We will remind them the tax loopholes they left in the area of research, which left gaps of several billion dollars in the Canadian economy. And who was bearing the burden, Madam Speaker? The Canadian workers, the workers from Quebec, all those who paid taxes to a Government who was supposed to be responsible but who almost drove Canada bankrupt, put Canada in such a financial state that industrialized countries in general did not trust it anymore; they put the people of Canada in such a situation that it did not trust them, and we saw what happened in 1984, because of the commitments they did not keep, because of the promises they had made for several elections but they never fulfilled.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, it is not a question of admitting that there was a mistake or not. The principles have not changed at all. In November 1984, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced that those who received income from pensions, which is considered income from employment, could not at the same time receive unemployment insurance benefits, which are also considered income from employment.
In other words, the established principle has remained the same. However, for reasons of understanding and as it seemed that, for all kinds of reasons, some people might sincerely and honestly not have understood our message before January 5, 1986, we decided to make this measure retroactive to January 5, 1986 and consider that these people had made in good faith a claim which should be honoured.
I would like to correct something which my colleague said. The principle has not changed in the last two years. You can say if you like that you have succeeded in making the Government change its mind. This is not important for us. What is important is to have been fair for the preretirees who honestly believed that the Government should respect its policy and to have decided not to apply to the letter a provision which these people might have misunderstood. This is what we recognize.
I repeat that we are continuing to apply the very same principles as before, and I would like the Hon. Member to remember it during the rest of this debate. The Government does not admit that anyone should receive benefits from two sources of employment income, in other words pension funds and the Unemployment Insurance Fund.

June 9, 1987

Government stands by that principle. If there is one group of Canadians who will know what that means and who will resent what the Government has done, it is members of the Armed Forces. We have heard Members on the government side say how proud and supportive they are of the Armed Forces. However, let us look at what this Bill does to members of the Armed Forces.
A man or woman joins the Armed Forces at the age of 18 or 20. As a member of the Armed Forces, unemployment insurance premiums are deducted from their pay. After 20 years that member of the Armed Forces retires, not because he or she wants to but because the regulation require them to do so. Therefore, at age 40 to 45 those people are forced out of the Armed Forces and immediately begin to draw their pensions. They do not have any choice but are required to do so.
That pension is too small to live on. Their home may have been in Winnipeg or Vancouver but they served a number of years in Halifax; Saint John, New Brunswick; or Ottawa and they want to move home. They have to relocate, buy a home, and find a job. It takes them some time to find a job. They are drawing a very small pension and, after having paid unemployment insurance premiums for 20 years, they should be able to get unemployment insurance benefits. They can get their benefits, but only after the deduction is made for their pension.
I received a letter from a Winnipeg resident who lives in the constituency of the Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine to whom he wrote first. The Member did not have the courtesy or decency to reply to the letter, perhaps because he did not care or perhaps because he did not know what to say. I will put this letter on the record and perhaps the Minister will give me a reply which I can send on to this person.
He says:
You are no doubt aware of the government action in altering the unemployment insurance (UI) program pertaining to severance pay and pension income.
1 am a member of the Canadian Armed Forces and will be retiring from the forces on t? Aug 85 after serving 33 years.
While the prospect of entering the civilian job market and establishing a second career does not greatly worry me, there are of course some personal concerns about the availability of suitable employment.
I have been contributing to UI since Armed Forces personnel were included. I currently contribute 46.84 each month to the scheme from which I can now claim no benefit. Under the government changes to the plan Armed Forces personnel have become victims of what may be called an insurance scam. We contribute premiums with no opportunity to benefit.
I was informed of the impending legislation at CFB Winnipeg in January '85 when making inquiries regarding my retirement benefits.
I wrote to my MP. Mr. Dan McKenzie, Winnipeg-Assiniboine. stating my view that the changes to the UI plan were unfair in that we were paying for nothing.
1 likened the situation to a family owning two cars. One car becomes damaged in an accident and the insurance company refused payment because the family has another car to drive.
I have paid into the UI, as Unemployment Insurance, not an income replacement scheme. I may soon be unemployed. Certainly 1 will have some income but it will be considerably less than I had anticipated should I be unable to secure employment.
Unemployment Insurance
Members of the forces have obviously had the foresight to maintain employment on a career basis with the aim of an annuity to assist in later life. We have served under conditions of service which do not apply to most civilian careers.
Frequent transfers, uprooting families from jobs and schools, rented and often sub-standard housing, hazardous work conditions and other vagaries of the profession.
At an age where a majority of civilian career workers are reaching an income and seniority peak, armed forces members are released from the service to attempt to establish a second career, normally at ages between 47 and 55.
Many members on release are in a transition period for some time. They move to a new location, they buy their first home, they are "Putting Down Roots" for the first time. Finding employment under these conditions is difficult. Not all military trades and professions are immediately transferable to civilian occupations. Unemployment Insurance always provided a "cushion" during that transition period.
Let me stop there for a moment. This member of the Forces obviously did not get a reply from his Member of Parliament, the Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie). Let me continue:
In a letter signed by Michael H. Wilson, Minister of Finance, 1 am informed that:
"The justification for the change in the treatment of pension income relates to the primary principle behind UI, which is to provide income protection to people who are without a job and without earnings. Someone receiving money from a previous employer in the form of a pension or separation pay cannot be said to be meeting these requirements. The change eliminates double payments and reinforces the objective of UI as an income replacement scheme".
Mr. Wilson's reference to "double payments" is nonsense. The Government is eliminating their "one payment" because 1 had the foresight to work at a career which provided some pension security. If it is the Government's intention to eliminate a percentage of the working population of Canada from UI benefits, it should also eliminate those same workers from paying premiums.
As you may detect in this letter, my reaction is one of anger. I feel cheated of even the possibility of drawing any benefit from unemployment insurance should I be unable to secure employment. As selfish as this view may appear, it is a view shared by a great many fellow service members.
He concludes his letter as follows:
It is a situation which makes me regret my 1984 vote for the Conservative party.
1 would like the Minister to tell me what answer 1 can give to satisfy this member of the Armed Forces and many others who feel exactly as he does.

The Government states that retired people with a pension-be honest now-will collect unemployment insurance benefits if their pension income is $5,000. Only those who are paid a $15,000 pension will not get unemployment insurance benefits. Benefits are progressively eliminated as the level of pension income goes up. Yes, but let us call a spade a spade. The older workers who are receiving $5,000 will collect unemployment insurance benefits. But it is clear that a person who is getting a $35,000 pension a year should not, a priori, collect $15,000 in unemployment insurance benefits just because he has paid premiums.
1 suggest that unemployment insurance benefits exist for people who have lost their jobs, who have no employment income and who are looking for a job. Elowever, we recognize that for those who have started a second career and who are paying premiums, it's not the principle but reality which has changed. It's reality which has changed, and you will have to admit that today, because people will have a second career which will last, not five or ten years, but 20 or 25 years, for when people reach age 50, they can start a career which may last 20 years, contributing premiums for 20 years. When they stop, according to the legislation which will be in force at the time, they will act accordingly.
We are trying to be logical, and I think we have been from the start; if we made adjustments, it is because we felt we had to take into account new facts such as a second career. The Government was motivated by fairness and justice for those to whom the new legislation and regulation have not been properly explained; that's why it added $65 million to establish a proper balance. I think that the Government has done its job. done its job.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BENEFIT ENTITLEMENT ADJUSTMENT (PENSION PAYMENTS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, if I understand the proposed amendment correctly, it would restrict the definition of pension to simply being pension under the Canada Pension Plan. As a result, an individual could not have his or her unemployment insurance benefits cut because they received pension arising out of employment or arising out of service in the Canadian Forces or any police force or under a provincial pension plan.
Under this amendment, unemployment insurance benefits could only be cut for those who receive pension under the Canada Pension Plan. As we know, that only takes effect at age 65. I see the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) nodding his head so 1 presume I understand his amendment correctly. It is a worth-while amendment because it restricts the harshness of this Bill, and while it is the best we can do on this clause, I think it is something which would certainly go a long way in making this Bill more acceptable. It
Unemployment Insurance
would no longer impinge upon people in the Armed Forces or police forces who were forced to retire early. It would not impinge upon those who work for Northern Electric or Bell Telephone who are forced to retire early, nor people who come under a provincial pension plan of any kind.
This raises the whole question of the real reason for this Bill. During the debate tonight, Hon. members from the government side have said this Bill is necessary-
An Hon. Member; Desirable.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BENEFIT ENTITLEMENT ADJUSTMENT (PENSION PAYMENTS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
-or desirable, whatever you wish. I was repeating some of the terminology used earlier this evening and during the day. Those Hon. Members said the Bill was necessary because unemployment insurance was never meant to be a pension plan. They implied that when people went on pension, they should not have the right to unemployment insurance benefits. I must point out again that the principle control mechanism in the Unemployment Insurance Act is that one must be ready and available for work. If a person in effect does retire, taking their early retirement pension, then no one is suggesting they should receive unemployment insurance benefits. A lot of people opposite do not seem to understand that. No one is suggesting that someone who is not ready, willing and available for work should receive unemployment insurance benefits.
The problem is for those people who receive an early retirement pension but are still ready and available for work because they are only age 45, 50, 55 or 60 years. They have a lot of good years left in them. They are receiving an early retirement pension and are ready and available for work. However, we have the control mechanism on abuse. If they are really using their unemployment benefits to retire, then the control mechanism is in the Act that they are not ready and available for work.
The discriminatory nature of all these measures-and I am glad the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt is restricting this definition of pension-is that while the Government has tried to cut back on employment insurance benefits for those who receive an early retirement pension, it does not cut back on their unemployment insurance if they retire early, do not get an early retirement pension, but are able to live on rents, dividends from stock or bonds, or types of income other than employment income. There was no attempt to do that. So it is very discriminatory.
I am pleased that the Hon. Member has put forward this amendment. We will support it because it restricts in a large measure the scope of this Bill. I give notice to the Minister that discrimination would still remain in the Bill and it would be essential to knock out all those provisions which discriminate between those who apply for their unemployment insurance benefits before January 1, 1986, and those who apply after. That is unacceptable and we will deal with that as soon as we have this amendment accepted by the Minister. I am sure he will see the reason for it.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I am rising in support of the amendment proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt. I would like to ask the Minister a question in connection with the amendment.
As the Minister knows, members of the Armed Forces and members of the RCMP have served Canada for many years. They have paid contributions into the unemployment insurance fund. These individuals, these members of the Canadian Armed Forces and the RCMP, have in fact assumed all along that because they had paid into this fund in good faith that they would then be in a position, if they were still actively looking for work and were unable to find employment, to draw upon unemployment insurance.
These individuals are forced to retire at an early age by the policies of the Armed Forces and the RCMP. The Special Committee on Equality Rights recommended that this type of forced early retirement be eliminated. But it has not been eliminated. The reality is that men and women in the Canadian Armed Forces and in the RCMP are in a position in which at the age of 45, 50, 55 they are thrown on to the job market. It is true that they have a pension, but in many cases they want to continue working.
As the correspondent to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North, pointed out, in many cases they have additional expenses involved in relocating from the Armed Forces, or relocating from where they may be serving with the RCMP. For example, they may be serving in Europe, in Lahr or Baden with the Armed Forces. They have assumed that they would have this money available, money which they paid into UI while they actively seek work.
The Minister represents men and women in the Armed Forces. He has members of the RCMP in his constituency. 1 have the honour of representing the constituency of Burnaby. I have a couple of hundred members of the Armed Forces in my riding who, in fact, are serving not only in Canada but in Europe as well. How can the Minister, and how can members of the Conservative Government and caucus, possibly support the betrayal, the breach of trust and the breach of contract which this Bill represents by denying to those members of the Canadian Armed Forces and the RCMP the right to apply for unemployment insurance if they are still actively looking for work when they are forced to retire from the forces and from the RCMP? How can the Minister possibly defend that policy?
Surely he recognizes that it is indefensible. Surely he recognizes that by supporting this amendment and by his Tory colleagues supporting it he would at least be keeping faith with the men and women of the Canadian Armed Forces and the RCMP who have served the country and who do not deserve to be stabbed in the back the way the Minister is doing.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BENEFIT ENTITLEMENT ADJUSTMENT (PENSION PAYMENTS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

Madam Chairman, of course I will not support the amendment. 1 am sorry. I have a great deal of respect for those people in the Armed Forces and in the RCMP. Giving UI or not to the people for whom we have a lot of respect is not the basis upon which we have to make such considerations. I agree with the Hon. Member that the people from the Armed Forces, from the RCMP and from the police forces across Canada have to take mandatory retirement sometimes at the age of 40 or 45 years. But those people have a pension. If the pension is too small, then, at that time, they have the right to make up the difference with their UI benefits. I refer to an amount lower than $15,000. That is what we call equity. At 40 or 45 years of age we are usually looking for another job. A great many times we have the possibility of getting a job, and at that time to requalify.
If we have to take those people out of the definition, then how can we give back that money to those people who requalified since January 5, 1986?
